answer: Many states favour one faith or one people in law: Pew found 43 countries with an official religion and more than 80 favouring one, including Denmark and the United Kingdom. In our reading Iran and Saudi Arabia are different in kind: their constitutions make Islamic law the source of state law. Germany's Basic Law counts as German people of German ethnic origin admitted as refugees or expellees; Israel's Law of Return gives Jews and their close relatives the right to immigrate. Israel's Declaration of Independence promises complete equality; critics of the 2018 Nation-State Law note it omits equality, while an INSS analysis finds nothing in it that explicitly permits discrimination. Scholars classify Israel differently: Smooha as an ethnic democracy, others as an ethnocracy. The United States offered naturalisation to free white persons in 1790, set quotas by nationality in 1924, and barred visa discrimination by race or nationality in 1965.

A third independent source for the Greek and Armenian descent rules (Greek and Armenian government pages do not count; GLOBALCIT and bpb are the readable reliable pages).

The Nation-State Law and the Law of Return on the Knesset's own site: the pages return nothing to the checker. The Law of Return text was read in a copy hosted by the International Commission of Jurists; the Nation-State Law rests on Middle East Eye, CNN and Freedom House (an unofficial translation hosted by Adalah, an advocacy group, was read but is not cited as the record).

A second reliable source for the scholarly classification of Israel (Smooha, Yiftachel): Smooha's article copy and Public Seminar are two sites; Yiftachel's own paper and the Wiley page blocked the checker.

National Academies Press (nationalacademies.org/read/21746/chapter/4) refuses the checker (HTTP 403), so every claim that rested on it was replaced by a statute text or other source; dropped: that the federal government did little to regulate immigration in the first century, and the 1917 Act. A person would need a readable source for both.

A scholar quoted as describing Israel as a liberal democracy (the Smooha abstract quotes that only as Israel's 'self-image'), and a named holder of the objection about non-citizens under Israeli control: neither found in a page the checker can read, so neither is in contested.

not_claimed: That preferring one people or religion is harmless: it can disadvantage minorities, and several of these states have been criticised for it.
That other countries' practices make any specific Israeli law just, or any other country's law just.
That Israel is, or is not, a democracy in every respect; the card gives indices and the scholarly disagreement.
That the United States has never been, or is now, closed to immigration; it states what the laws said when.

answer_claims.says: Many states favour one faith or one people in law.
Pew found 43 countries with an official religion and more than 80 favouring one, including Denmark and the United Kingdom.
In our reading Iran and Saudi Arabia are different in kind: their constitutions make Islamic law the source of state law.
Germany's Basic Law counts as German people of German ethnic origin admitted as refugees or expellees.
Israel's Law of Return gives Jews and their close relatives the right to immigrate.
Israel's Declaration of Independence promises complete equality.
Critics of the 2018 Nation-State Law note it omits equality, while an INSS analysis finds nothing in it that explicitly permits discrimination.
Scholars classify Israel differently: Smooha as an ethnic democracy, others as an ethnocracy.
The United States offered naturalisation to free white persons in 1790, set quotas by nationality in 1924, and barred visa discrimination by race or nationality in 1965.

skeptic.notes: Read the statutes themselves: 1790 (1 Stat. 103), 1882, 1924 (43 Stat. 153), 1952, 1965 (79 Stat. 911) quotes are in the Statutes at Large and in context; Iran art. 4 and Saudi art. 7 verified on Constitute; Law of Return, Article 116, Palestine Basic Law, Irish s.27 verified. must-fix: the required 'contested' content is incomplete. (1) No scholar is quoted as describing Israel as a liberal democracy: Smooha's abstract mentions 'liberal democracy' only as Israel's self-image. (2) The objection about non-citizens under Israeli control has no named holder; the two Freedom House lines are data, not a quoted position. Freedom House's own page says the Israel score does not reflect conditions in the West Bank and Gaza, which belongs in this entry. A critic from either side will say the card omits the strongest form of the opposing view. must-fix: the Yiftachel 'ethnocracy' position is quoted only second-hand (Public Seminar, by Shaul and Yehuda Magid); Yiftachel himself was not read. must-fix: the 2018 Nation-State Law (fact 12) is not read from the Knesset or any official text; it rests on Middle East Eye's translation (labelled now), CNN and Freedom House. The Law of Return's is_record source (ICJ copy) holds only the 1950 text; the 1970 amendment (grandchildren, spouses, definition of Jew) was read only in Jewish Virtual Library and the IRB of Canada. must-fix: fact 0 is flagged record, but its two reliable 'readers' (Springer on a 2008 survey of 177 countries, Cambridge on Fox) report different surveys, not Pew's; Pew has no independent reader. Facts 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 14, 15, 17, 19, 21 fail the gate's source rule; fact 4's third source (Pew) says only that Saudi Arabia favours Islam, not that religious law is state law; fact 15 is Freedom House alone. should-fix: fact 18 stated only the 1890-census formula; the same section sets the 1927 national-origins formula (added). Fact 6 said Article 116 itself covers late emigrants; the article's text does not mention them (reworded to attribute to bpb and the law firm). The 1965 Act is quoted for non-discrimination 'except as specifically provided'; the per-country ceilings remain, and the card does not say so (nit-to-should). should-fix: Pew's 2017 count includes states beyond Christianity and Islam; the card does not say whether Pew counts Israel or Judaism, which a critic will ask.
